narrativeReportMd:
# Provenance R4→R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Breaking local Provenance changes were found. The highest-impact R4→R6 breaks are removal/splitting of `Provenance.reason`, removal of the required `entity.role` code `derivation`, and removal of Device/RelatedPerson from `agent.onBehalfOf`. R6 also adds stricter delegation constraints and several R6-only fields that complicate down-conversion.

## Scope
This report compares the R4 4.0.1 and R6 6.0.0-ballot4 core `StructureDefinition/Provenance` resources and local terminology needed to interpret Provenance bindings. Inherited Resource/DomainResource/Element/Extension changes are listed out of scope and not counted as findings.

## Main migration themes
The R6 model clarifies Provenance semantics around authorization, delegation, workflow context, patient/encounter context, and functional versus structural agent roles. These changes improve expressiveness but require explicit migration rules rather than mechanical field renames.

## Highest-impact findings
- `Provenance:ELEMENT_PRESENCE_OR_IDENTITY:Provenance.reason:be90a8`: `reason` is gone and must be mapped to `authorization`, `why`, extensions, or manual review.
- `Provenance:TERMINOLOGY_BINDING:Provenance.entity.role:54055e`: the required entity-role vocabulary changed, removing `derivation` and adding `instantiates`/`other`.
- `Provenance:REFERENCE_TARGET:Provenance.agent.onBehalfOf:6c650f`: `agent.onBehalfOf` no longer permits Device or RelatedPerson and now specifically represents delegated authority.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important for reason splitting, entity-role code mapping, delegation/self-reference constraints, new context elements, and role terminology semantics. These areas can remain structurally valid while changing audit, authorization, or accountability meaning.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several breaks could have been softened with deprecation, warning constraints, transitional value sets, or published cross-version extensions. The likely design goal—clearer Provenance semantics—is understandable, but implementers need migration policy for historical R4 data and R6→R4 exchange.

## Follow-up analysis
Base Resource/DomainResource/Element/Extension changes should be handled by their own artifact reports. Terminology expansions, official diffs, and ballot/Jira notes would improve mapping confidence for PurposeOfUse, participation-role-type, and security-role-type changes.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: Provenance has several local R4→R6 breaking changes: `reason` was removed/split, the required `entity.role` code set changed, and `agent.onBehalfOf` removed Device/RelatedPerson targets. The largest R6→R4 risks are optional `recorded`, new context elements, and new agent target types. Confidence is high for structure-level changes; terminology mapping details need official expansions and change notes.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is less about a single cardinality tightening and more about **semantic remodeling**: reason/authorization/why, functional vs structural agent roles, stricter delegation rules, and a changed entity role vocabulary. R4→R6 pipelines need explicit transforms for removed fields and invalid codes; R6→R4 pipelines need extensions or rejection policies for new fields and missing `recorded`.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high because both assigned StructureDefinitions are present and the most important differences are computable in the snapshots/differentials. Confidence is medium for exact terminology and design-intent judgements where external value-set expansions, ConceptMaps, official diffs, or Jira notes would improve the assessment.

findings.title: Provenance.reason was removed and split/reframed as authorization plus why

oldState.summary: R4 had Provenance.reason as 0..* CodeableConcept with an extensible PurposeOfUse binding.

binding.description: The reason the activity took place.

semanticText.definition: The reason that the activity was taking place.

oldState.narrativeMd: `Provenance.reason` carried coded reasons, commonly including purpose-of-use style codes, and allowed multiple CodeableConcept values.

newState.summary: R6 has no Provenance.reason. It adds Provenance.authorization (0..* CodeableConcept, example PurposeOfUse binding) and Provenance.why (0..1 markdown, alias reason).

binding.description: The authorized purposeOfUse for the activity.

semanticText.short: Authorization (purposeOfUse) related to the event / Why was the event performed?
semanticText.definition: Authorization records security context; why records textual rationale.

newState.narrativeMd: `Provenance.authorization` appears to take over the security/purpose-of-use portion of R4 `reason`, while `Provenance.why` is a separate free-text rationale. The R4 path itself is gone.

facts.note: Same CodeableConcept type and same v3-PurposeOfUse value set, but binding strength changed from extensible to example and semantics are authorization/security context.
Alias reason, but markdown 0..1 cannot losslessly carry repeated CodeableConcept codings.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 definitions and aliases indicate a split rather than a simple rename: coded purpose-of-use content maps most closely to `authorization`, while general explanatory text maps to `why`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 instance containing the JSON member `reason` uses an element that no longer exists in the R6 base resource and will fail strict R6 validation or generated-model parsing. R6 `authorization` and `why` are likewise not base R4 elements. The change is also not a lossless rename because multiplicity, datatype, binding strength, and semantics changed.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Purpose-of-use and audit rationale can affect access-control, audit, and trust decisions; mis-mapping it can change security interpretation even if clinical payloads are unchanged.

justification.inferredGoal: Separate authorization/security context from free-text explanatory rationale.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain R4 `reason` as the coded authorization/security-context element, with a clearer definition, and add `why` only for textual rationale.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Separating authorization/security context from a human-readable rationale is a reasonable R6 goal, but the hard break comes from removing the R4 path. Because R4 `reason` already had the same repeated CodeableConcept shape and PurposeOfUse binding family as R6 `authorization`, the goal could likely have been met by clarifying the old element rather than invalidating existing instances.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have kept `Provenance.reason` as the 0..* coded authorization or purpose-of-use field, marked it deprecated or given it an authorization alias, and added `Provenance.why` for markdown rationale. That avoids a duplicate coded same-resource field if `authorization` is not also introduced; the tradeoff is living with the older, less specific name and relying on definitions and guidance to narrow its semantics.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves most R4 instances but keeps a less precise legacy name and may leave some historically broad reasons semantically ambiguous.

evidence.detail: R4 defines `reason` as 0..* CodeableConcept.
R6 has no element with id `Provenance.reason`.
R6 adds `authorization` as 0..* CodeableConcept with an example PurposeOfUse binding.
R6 adds `why` as 0..1 markdown and gives it alias `reason`.

r6NotRepresentableInR4Json.why: Treatment-related access as recorded by the source system.

migrationExampleJson.why: Original R4 Provenance.reason display/text may need review before placing it in markdown.

examples.examplesMd: Fragments are illustrative. A production transform should inspect each R4 CodeableConcept: coded purpose-of-use/security context usually belongs in `authorization`; narrative-only rationale may belong in `why`; repeated coded reasons cannot always be represented by the single markdown `why` element.

findings.narrativeMd: `Provenance.reason` is no longer a valid R6 element. R6 introduces `authorization` for purpose-of-use/security context and `why` for textual rationale, so this is a split/reframe rather than a mechanical rename. Implementations that persisted, indexed, validated, or generated accessors for `reason` need explicit migration logic.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `reason` are old-valid/new-invalid under strict R6 validation because the element is absent. R6 instances using `authorization` or `why` are not directly representable in base R4. Compatibility is further complicated because R4 allowed multiple coded CodeableConcept reasons, while R6 `why` is single markdown and `authorization` has a weaker example binding.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not blindly rename `reason` to `why`. Classify each R4 reason value: map purpose-of-use/security codes to `authorization`, convert only appropriate human-readable rationale to `why`, and preserve unmappable codings in an extension or cross-version mapping note. Test multiple reasons, coded-only reasons, text-only reasons, and round-trip R6→R4 behavior.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The conceptual split is understandable, but removal of `reason` was not the only option. Keeping a deprecated `reason` element or defining an explicit cross-version extension would have allowed older instances to validate while new systems adopted clearer fields.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The supplied package did not include an official change note explaining the split; the mapping judgement is inferred from R6 element names, aliases, definitions, and bindings.

findings.title: Required Provenance.entity.role code set removed derivation and added instantiates/other

oldState.summary: R4 role was required code bound to ValueSet/provenance-entity-role|4.0.1.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R4 CodeSystem is complete and contains derivation, revision, quotation, source, and removal.

oldState.narrativeMd: Because the binding is required, R4 role values had to be drawn from the R4 Provenance entity role code system.

newState.summary: R6 role remains required but the complete code system contains revision, quotation, source, instantiates, removal, and other.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: The local R6 CodeSystem is complete. Shared codes also have revised definitions, especially `source` and `revision`.

semanticText.short: revision | quotation | source | instantiates | removal | other

newState.narrativeMd: `derivation` is no longer a legal required-binding code; `instantiates` and `other` are new R6 legal codes.

impact.impactRationaleMd: `Provenance.entity.role` is a required code with a required binding. Any R4 entity role of `derivation` becomes invalid in R6. Conversely, R6 `instantiates` or `other` cannot be represented as valid base R4 role codes. Generated enums and switch statements are especially exposed.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Entity role controls whether referenced material is treated as source, revision, removal, or another provenance relationship; a wrong mapping can change audit interpretation.

justification.inferredGoal: Flatten and clarify provenance entity roles, and add explicit roles for instantiation and otherwise-unclassified usage.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `derivation` as a deprecated valid code while adding R6 `instantiates` and `other`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying entity roles and adding more precise choices is reasonable, but removing a code from a required binding directly invalidates R4 instances that used `derivation`. Keeping the old code available while encouraging newer codes would have preserved validation compatibility without blocking the R6 vocabulary expansion.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The base R6 CodeSystem/ValueSet could have retained `derivation` with deprecated or legacy wording and added `instantiates` and `other` as preferred alternatives. Implementers could then migrate broad `derivation` uses gradually. The main downside is that the less precise code might remain in data and picklists longer, but that tradeoff is moderate compared with a required-binding validation break.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The old broad code would persist in the required binding and may delay precise mapping, but preserving it is a low-cost compatibility path.

evidence.detail: R4 binding is required to `ValueSet/provenance-entity-role|4.0.1`.
R6 binding is required to `ValueSet/provenance-entity-role|6.0.0-ballot4`.
R4 complete CodeSystem includes `derivation`, `revision`, `quotation`, `source`, and `removal`.
R6 complete CodeSystem includes `revision`, `quotation`, `source`, `instantiates`, `removal`, and `other`.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is not universally correct. R4 `derivation` must be reviewed and mapped to the closest R6 role based on actual provenance semantics.

findings.narrativeMd: The required entity role vocabulary changed. The R4 broad `derivation` code is gone, while R6 adds `instantiates` and `other` and revises the code definitions. Because the binding is required, this is a direct validation and code-generation break, not merely a display-text change.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `entity.role = "derivation"` can become invalid in R6. R6 instances with `entity.role = "instantiates"` or `"other"` are invalid in R4. Strict validators should catch this through the required binding; generated enum models may fail at parse time or route values to unknown-code branches.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all `Provenance.entity.role` values. Map R4 `derivation` only after checking whether the entity was a source, a revised version, an instantiating definition, or some other relationship. Preserve original codes in an extension or audit note when the transform is uncertain. Add round-trip tests for each role code.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A compatible path was available by retaining `derivation` as deprecated while adding R6-specific codes. That would have avoided invalidating old instances but would have allowed less precise data to persist.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Code comparison used the local complete CodeSystem resources rather than a live terminology server expansion.

findings.title: Provenance.agent.onBehalfOf no longer permits Device or RelatedPerson and now represents delegation

oldState.summary: R4 onBehalfOf could reference Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Patient, Device, or Organization.

semanticText.definition: The individual, device, or organization for whom the change was made.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 modeled `onBehalfOf` as the party for whom a change was made, including devices and related persons.

newState.summary: R6 onBehalfOf can reference Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, CareTeam, Patient, Group, or HealthcareService; Device and RelatedPerson are removed.

semanticText.definition: The agent that delegated authority to perform the activity performed by the agent.who element.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 reframes the field as delegation authority and removes two R4 reference target types while adding team/group/service targets.

facts.oldValue: for whom the change was made

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct reference-target break for R4 instances whose `onBehalfOf` points to a Device or RelatedPerson. R6 additions also create R6 instances that R4 reference-target validation and generated type unions cannot represent. The semantic shift to delegation means even target types that remain legal may need review.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Delegation and representation affect accountability and audit interpretation; incorrect migration can assign responsibility to the wrong actor.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify `onBehalfOf` as delegation and align target types with agents capable of delegation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain Device and RelatedPerson during transition, or add a delegation-specific successor while keeping legacy `onBehalfOf`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of making `onBehalfOf` specifically mean delegated authority is reasonable for audit accountability. A less-breaking design exists, but retaining the old broad target set would continue to validate assertions that may not represent delegation at all, so the breaking target cleanup is probably justified even though official intent evidence was not supplied.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A partial base alternative would decouple the semantic change from the target-list cleanup: keep Device and RelatedPerson as deprecated targets with warning guidance, or add a new delegation-specific element while preserving the old `onBehalfOf` shape. That would protect old instances, but it creates same-resource ambiguity about which representation carries the delegator and risks old non-delegation usage persisting indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves legacy data but leaves ambiguous delegation semantics, duplicate representations, and accountability risk.

evidence.detail: R4 target profiles include Device and RelatedPerson.
R6 target profiles omit Device and RelatedPerson and add CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService.
R4 definition describes the party for whom the change was made.
evidence.quote: The individual, device, or organization for whom the change was made.

evidence.detail: R6 definition describes delegated authority.
evidence.quote: The agent that delegated authority to perform the activity performed by the agent.who element.

examples.examplesMd: The first fragment is structurally aligned with R4 target profiles but violates the R6 `onBehalfOf` target set. The second uses a new R6 target type that R4 did not permit.

findings.narrativeMd: `Provenance.agent.onBehalfOf` changed both its allowed reference targets and its meaning. Existing R4 records using a Device or RelatedPerson as the represented party no longer fit the R6 base target list, and retained target types should be reviewed because the R6 field specifically means delegated authority.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Strict R6 validators can reject `onBehalfOf.reference` values whose resource type is Device or RelatedPerson. R6 CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService references are not valid R4 targets. Generated model unions or profile validators may surface this as parse, assignment, or validation failures.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Find all R4 `agent.onBehalfOf` references to Device or RelatedPerson. Determine whether they represent a delegating agent, a beneficiary, a device acting as who, or contextual information that belongs elsewhere or in an extension. For retained types, test accountability logic because the R6 definition is delegation-specific.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Removing target types from the base resource is strongly breaking. A profile-level restriction or staged deprecation would have given implementations a path to clean data without rejecting existing instances immediately.

findings.title: Provenance.agent.who adds CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService reference targets

oldState.summary: R4 who targets Practitioner, PractitionerRole, RelatedPerson, Patient, Device, and Organization.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed six actor target resource types.

newState.summary: R6 keeps all R4 who targets and adds CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 broadens actors to include teams, groups, and healthcare services.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances are not invalidated because no R4 target was removed. The risk is in R6 data flowing to R4 systems and in generated code that assumes a closed set of actor resource types.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow non-individual actors such as care teams, groups, and healthcare services to be recorded directly as Provenance agents.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking base alternative is needed because R6 retains every R4 `agent.who` target and only adds new targets.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Allowing CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService as Provenance agents is a reasonable expressiveness improvement, and the R6 base target widening preserves R4-valid instances. The remaining issue is older R4 consumers receiving newer R6 data, not avoidable R4-to-R6 breakage.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Backport extensions or conversion policies can help R4 recipients carry the new actor types, but those are migration mitigations. They are not backward-compatible alternatives to a breaking base R6 design because this change is already forward-compatible for R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: New targets create R6-to-R4 mapping work for older consumers but do not invalidate R4 instances.

evidence.detail: R4 target set has six resource types.
R6 adds CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService and retains the R4 target types.

examples.examplesMd: This R6 fragment uses a valid R6 actor target that R4 base Provenance did not permit.

findings.narrativeMd: `agent.who` is wider in R6. This does not break existing R4 instances, but R4 consumers and generated SDKs that model `who` as a closed union need to handle CareTeam, Group, and HealthcareService when receiving R6 data.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6 validation is safe for this target-list change. R6→R4 conversion is not lossless when `who` uses one of the new targets unless an extension, contained proxy, or policy-specific mapping is used.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated type unions, reference validators, and business rules to accept the new R6 actor types. When downgrading to R4, use an explicit extension or reject records where the actor cannot be represented without changing accountability semantics.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding targets is the normal forward-compatible way to broaden a reference. The unavoidable compatibility issue is with older R4 consumers that cannot natively represent the new actors.

findings.title: R6 adds local error constraints preventing self or circular delegation patterns on Provenance.agent

oldState.summary: R4 Provenance.agent had no Provenance-specific invariants beyond inherited ele-1.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed `who` and `onBehalfOf` combinations without local self-delegation checks.

newState.summary: R6 adds prov-1 through prov-4 as error constraints on Provenance.agent.

constraints.human: Who and onBehalfOf cannot be the same
constraints.expression: who.resolve().exists() and onBehalfOf.resolve().exists() implies who.resolve() != onBehalfOf.resolve()

constraints.human: If who is a PractitionerRole, onBehalfOf can't reference the same Practitioner
If who is an organization, onBehalfOf can't be a PractitionerRole within that organization
If who is an organization, onBehalfOf can't be a healthcare service within that organization

newState.narrativeMd: R6 validates delegation relationships and rejects several cases where the actor and delegator collapse to the same underlying party.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These are error-level invariants, so affected R4 instances can become invalid in R6. The reason this is marked Potential rather than unconditional is that the FHIRPath expressions depend on `resolve()`; validators that cannot resolve the referenced resources may not detect the violation.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The constraints protect accountability semantics by preventing the delegating and acting parties from being effectively the same.

justification.inferredGoal: Prevent nonsensical or misleading delegation assertions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Introduce prov-1 through prov-4 first as warnings or profile constraints before making them base error constraints.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Preventing self-delegation and circular delegation is a reasonable accountability goal. The stricter error constraints can invalidate some R4 instances, but a softer rollout would leave misleading delegation assertions conformant in the base resource, so the breakage is probably justified rather than clearly avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A partial alternative would define these checks as warning or best-practice constraints, or enforce them only in R6 profiles initially. That would reduce migration failures for legacy data, but validators and trading partners could not rely on base Provenance to exclude the problematic delegation patterns.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Warnings preserve legacy data but do not guarantee clean delegation semantics; base errors can reject rare but misleading historical assertions.

evidence.detail: R4 has no prov-* constraints on Provenance.agent.
R6 adds prov-1, prov-2, prov-3, and prov-4 as error constraints.
evidence.quote: Who and onBehalfOf cannot be the same

examples.examplesMd: With both references resolvable to the same contained Practitioner, the fragment illustrates prov-1. External references may only be caught when the validator has resolver access.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds four Provenance-specific error constraints to `agent`. They disallow self-delegation and several equivalent same-party delegation patterns involving PractitionerRole, Practitioner, Organization, and HealthcareService. This can invalidate old data that used `onBehalfOf` loosely.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance can become invalid in R6 if a validator can resolve `who` and `onBehalfOf` and the resolved resources violate prov-1 through prov-4. Static JSON-schema-like validators may miss these constraints; full FHIRPath validation with reference resolution is needed.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Run R6 validation with reference resolution enabled on representative Provenance data. Where violations are found, remove redundant `onBehalfOf`, correct the referenced delegator, or preserve the original assertion in an extension if it reflected a local business convention rather than true delegation.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The checks improve data quality but could have been introduced as warnings or profile constraints first. Base error constraints maximize interoperability at the cost of stricter migration requirements.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Constraint impact depends on validator resolver behavior and availability of referenced resources.

findings.title: Provenance.recorded minimum cardinality decreased from 1 to 0

semanticText.definition: The instant of time at which the activity was recorded.

oldState.narrativeMd: `recorded` was mandatory in base R4 Provenance.

newState.summary: R6 makes recorded optional while retaining type instant and max 1.

semanticText.definition: The date and time at which the provenance information was recorded / updated, whether in the FHIR Provenance resource or in some other form that is later communicated in the FHIR Provenance.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This widens R6, so R4 instances with `recorded` remain valid with respect to this element. The break appears when R6 data omits `recorded`: base R4 requires it, and generated R4 models may assume a non-null timestamp.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow Provenance to be communicated when the recording timestamp is unknown or recorded elsewhere.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 definition indicates a plausible goal of allowing Provenance when the recording time is unknown or captured outside the FHIR instance. Because this is a cardinality relaxation, it does not make R4-valid instances invalid in R6; the compatibility concern is downstream conversion to R4.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Keeping `recorded` at min=1 would preserve easier R4 round-tripping, but it is not a less-breaking R4-to-R6 alternative because the R6 change is already forward-compatible. It would instead block the R6 goal of allowing provenance records without a known in-resource recorded instant.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6 can represent unknown or externally recorded timestamps; R4 consumers need an explicit policy for missing `recorded`.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: relaxing `recorded` from mandatory to optional preserves R4 instances and primarily affects R6-to-R4 conversion.

evidence.detail: R4 min cardinality is 1.
R6 min cardinality is 0.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example shows the kind of backfill R4 needs, but a fabricated timestamp can be misleading and should be distinguishable from an actual recorded time.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 no longer requires `recorded`. This is not an R4→R6 validation break, but it is a significant downgrade and code-generation issue because R4 Provenance always had a recording instant.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Valid R6 instances can omit `recorded` and therefore fail R4 validation. R4 generated models may expose `recorded` as required/non-null and fail when ingesting R6. Existing R4 instances are not invalidated by this relaxation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6→R4 conversion, decide whether missing `recorded` should block conversion, be backfilled from `meta.lastUpdated` or another audit timestamp, or be carried with an extension explaining that the true recorded time is unknown. Avoid silently fabricating audit timestamps.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Relaxing cardinality is backward-compatible in the forward direction but creates an unavoidable representability gap for old R4 consumers. A profile could require `recorded` for exchange partners that need R4 round-trip compatibility.

findings.title: R6 adds optional basedOn, patient, and encounter context elements

oldState.summary: R4 had no base Provenance.basedOn, Provenance.patient, or Provenance.encounter elements.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 systems typically inferred workflow, patient, and encounter context from target resources, agents, entities, compartments, or extensions.

newState.summary: R6 adds basedOn 0..* Reference(Resource), patient 0..1 Reference(Patient), and encounter 0..1 Reference(Encounter).

semanticText.requirements: Context links can affect tracing, workflow, compartments, and access control.

newState.narrativeMd: `patient` is a summary element and has SHALL/SHALL NOT accuracy requirements in its definition text; `encounter` and `basedOn` add workflow and encounter context.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not invalidate R4 instances during R4→R6 validation. They do, however, create new JSON members and semantic obligations that R4 parsers, generated classes, search/index logic, and access-control rules will not understand without mapping.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: `patient` and `encounter` context may drive compartment and access-control decisions; dropping them during down-conversion can change authorization behavior.

justification.inferredGoal: Make workflow, patient, and encounter context explicit on Provenance.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: optional R6 context additions do not invalidate R4 instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Making workflow, patient, and encounter context explicit on Provenance is a reasonable R6 design goal, and adding these elements as optional content is forward-compatible for R4-to-R6 validation. The break is only for R6 content moving back into an R4 base model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R4 extensions and cross-version transforms are useful migration tools for carrying these new context links to older systems, but they are not less-breaking alternatives to a base R6 design. The base R6 additions already preserve old R4 instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Native context fields improve R6 interoperability but need extension mapping, loss policy, or rejection when sending R6 data to R4.

evidence.detail: R6 adds basedOn 0..* Reference(Resource).
R6 adds patient 0..1 Reference(Patient) and marks it summary.
R6 adds encounter 0..1 Reference(Encounter).

examples.examplesMd: Base R4 Provenance has no native places for these three members; R4 conversion needs extensions or derived context.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds explicit workflow, patient, and encounter context to Provenance. These additions are not old-instance breaking, but they matter for R6 data exchange because R4 systems will otherwise drop context that may be needed for auditing and access decisions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4→R6 validation is safe. R6→R4 validation fails if these unknown members are left in a base R4 instance, and silently dropping them can change semantics. Generated R4 models need extension mapping or a rejection policy.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map these elements to well-defined R4 extensions when down-converting, or reconstruct them from target resources only when deterministic. Pay particular attention to `patient` because the R6 requirements text says it SHALL be accurate when populated and SHALL NOT be populated when the target data has no subject.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Adding optional elements is relatively compatible, but R4 round-trip compatibility would require published cross-version extensions and explicit transformation rules.

findings.title: Several local Provenance elements became summary elements in R6

oldState.summary: R4 marked target, recorded, agent.who, agent.type, and entity.role as summary-relevant among local Provenance elements; activity, agent, entity, and occurred[x] were not summary.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `_summary=true` responses were less likely to include the full local agent/entity backbones or activity timing.

newState.summary: R6 marks activity, agent, entity, and occurred[x] as summary; new patient is also summary.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 summary projections can include more Provenance content, including repeating backbone elements.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Summary flags do not change instance validity or wire syntax. They can change REST `_summary=true`, generated summary serializers, indexing, caching, and payload-size assumptions.

justification.inferredGoal: Expose more clinically and operationally useful Provenance context in summary views.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The elements newly marked as summary carry important provenance context, so exposing them in summary views is reasonable. Since the flags do not change the validity of R4 instances or the base wire shape, this is not an avoidable R4-to-R6 base-design break.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Servers and clients can mitigate runtime surprises by documenting summary behavior or requesting explicit `_elements`, but those are operational controls. There is no backward-compatible base-design alternative to assess for old-instance validation because no R4 instance is invalidated.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: More useful summaries may increase payload size and privacy exposure; explicit `_elements` or server policy can manage exact projections.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: summary flags affect projection/API behavior, not instance validity.

evidence.detail: R4 local activity, agent, entity, and occurred[x] are not summary.
R6 local activity, agent, entity, occurred[x], and new patient are summary elements.

examples.examplesMd: No JSON instance fragment is needed because summary flags affect projection behavior, not validity.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 expands which Provenance elements are considered summary content. The practical effect is in API responses and generated serializers rather than validation: clients asking for summaries may see more Provenance data than in R4.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: No R4-valid instance becomes invalid. The change can alter runtime behavior for `_summary=true`, `_elements`, summary serializers, caches, and clients that assumed summary Provenance omitted agent/entity details.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review server summary projection tests and client expectations. Treat this as an API behavior change: verify payload size, privacy exposure of agents/entities, and UI assumptions for summary-mode Provenance.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This is a metadata behavior change rather than an avoidable structural break. Implementations can mitigate by documenting summary behavior and using explicit `_elements` when exact projections are required.

findings.title: Provenance.agent.role changed to structural-role semantics and a much narrower example value set

oldState.summary: R4 role was an example binding to ValueSet/security-role-type with general security/agent role wording.

semanticText.definition: The function of the agent with respect to the activity. The security role enabling the agent with respect to the activity.
semanticText.comment: For example: doctor, nurse, clerk, etc.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 examples and value set pointed to a broad security role type collection.

newState.summary: R6 role is described as structural competency and has an example binding to ValueSet/security-role-type-example.

semanticText.definition: The structural roles of the agent indicating the agent's competency. The security role enabling the agent with respect to the activity.
semanticText.requirements: Structural roles reflect the structural aspects of relationships between entities.

newState.narrativeMd: The local R6 example value set includes only the example security structural roles code system, whose complete local code system has two concepts.

facts.newValue: structural roles of the agent indicating competency

impact.impactRationaleMd: The binding remains example, so base validation should not reject old role codings solely because of the value set change. The risk is semantic and runtime: systems that treated `agent.role` as a functional or broad security role may need to distinguish it from R6 structural role semantics and from `agent.type` functional role semantics.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Agent role data can affect accountability, authorization, and audit display.

justification.inferredGoal: Separate structural roles/competencies from functional participation roles.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the element shape and example binding do not by themselves make R4 `agent.role` instances invalid.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying the distinction between structural role and functional participation role is a reasonable R6 goal. Because `agent.role` remains a CodeableConcept with an example binding, the change is a semantic and runtime migration concern rather than a hard R4-to-R6 validation break.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Implementers may keep broader local role value sets, ConceptMaps, or compatibility picklists while adopting the R6 structural-role interpretation. Those mitigations can reduce operational churn, but they are not backward-compatible alternatives to a breaking base R6 design because the base R6 element does not reject R4 role codings solely due to the example binding.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Terminology picklists, audit logic, and authorization logic still need review, but retaining broader local code sets is migration policy rather than a less-breaking base design.

evidence.detail: R4 example value set is `security-role-type`.
R6 example value set is `security-role-type-example`.
R6 requirements define structural roles and cite ISO role models.
The local R6 example CodeSystem has regulated-health-professionals and non-regulated-health-professionals.

examples.examplesMd: Because the binding is example, examples are semantic rather than validation examples: old local role codes may still be syntactically valid but no longer align with the intended R6 structural-role axis.

findings.narrativeMd: `agent.role` is still a CodeableConcept with an example binding, but R6 repurposes the guidance toward structural roles/competencies and changes the example value set. This can break application logic that used R4 `role` for broad operational or functional participation categories.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Base validation is unlikely to reject R4 codes because both bindings are example. The compatibility risk is semantic, enum/value-set helper behavior, UI labels, and authorization/audit rules that interpret role codes according to the old R4 examples.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review every use of `agent.role`. Move functional participation concepts to `agent.type` where appropriate, keep structural competency/position concepts in `agent.role`, and update terminology picklists and mappings. Do not infer that the two-code R6 example value set is an exhaustive allowed set.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 clarification could have been introduced through narrative guidance while preserving the old example value set, but the stronger semantic separation likely improves long-term interoperability.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: A live terminology expansion would improve confidence about the full intended example sets, especially for external security-role terminology.

findings.title: Provenance.activity and agent.type bindings were weakened and retargeted to different example value sets

oldState.summary: R4 activity and agent.type had extensible bindings.

binding.description: R4 activity used provenance-activity-type; R4 agent.type used provenance-agent-type.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 validators could apply extensible-binding expectations to activity and agent participation type.

newState.summary: R6 changes both bindings to example and retargets agent.type to participation-role-type; activity keeps the same value set URL but its compose changed to ISO 21089 lifecycle concepts.

binding.description: R6 activity uses a changed provenance-activity-type value set; R6 agent.type uses participation-role-type.

semanticText.definition: agent.type is now the Functional Role of the agent with respect to the activity.

newState.narrativeMd: The R6 conformance burden is weaker, but terminology picklists and role semantics shift.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Weakening extensible to example reduces base validation strictness, so old instances are not rejected for this reason. However, terminology services, generated enums, picklists, decision logic, and conformance tests may behave differently because the recommended code sets and role semantics changed.

justification.inferredGoal: Align activity with lifecycle terminology and clarify agent.type as functional participation role.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: weakening the bindings to example means R4 codes are not invalidated by base R6 terminology validation.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Aligning activity and agent type with lifecycle and functional-role terminology is a reasonable goal, and weakening the binding strength avoids a hard terminology validation break. The remaining compatibility risk is semantic/runtime behavior in systems that generated closed code lists or applied local extensible-binding policy.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A transitional union value set or official ConceptMap would make migration safer, but that would be supporting guidance rather than a necessary less-breaking base design. Since R6 uses example bindings here, the base resource already avoids invalidating R4 instances on terminology membership alone.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Terminology picklists, enums, analytics, and mappings may need updates; transitional value sets or ConceptMaps are migration aids.

evidence.detail: R4 activity binding is extensible to `provenance-activity-type`.
R6 activity binding is example to `provenance-activity-type`.
R4 compose includes DocumentCompletion, ActCode, DataOperation, and ParticipationType; R6 compose includes selected iso-21089-lifecycle codes.
R4 agent.type binding is extensible to `provenance-agent-type`.
R6 agent.type binding is example to `participation-role-type` and definition says Functional Role.

examples.examplesMd: No old-valid/new-invalid instance is expected solely from these binding changes because the R6 binding strength is weaker. The examples to test are terminology-service, picker, and enum-generation cases.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 weakens important Provenance terminology bindings from extensible to example while also changing the recommended code sets and clarifying `agent.type` as functional role. This is not a hard instance break, but it is a conformance and runtime migration risk.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Strict R6 validation should not reject R4 codes solely due to these bindings because example bindings are non-restrictive. Systems that generated enums from value sets, used extensible-binding warnings as policy, or assumed R4 activity/agent-type code sets may still break or change behavior.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review terminology picklists, enum generation, validation policy, and analytics using `activity` or `agent.type`. Map R4 activity codes to R6 lifecycle concepts where possible and distinguish `agent.type` functional participation from `agent.role` structural competency.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The spec avoided hard terminology breaks by weakening the binding. More explicit ConceptMaps or transitional union value sets would make migration safer without over-constraining R6.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: External value set expansions and official ConceptMaps were not available locally, so detailed code-level mapping is limited.

findings.title: Provenance.entity.agent definition changed from generated-entity responsibility to used-entity responsibility

oldState.summary: R4 said the shorthand meant the agent was responsible for the activity which generated the entity.

semanticText.definition: The entity is attributed to an agent to express the agent's responsibility for that entity, possibly along with other agents. This description can be understood as shorthand for saying that the agent was responsible for the activity which generated the entity.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 wording points to provenance of the entity as generated output.

newState.summary: R6 says the shorthand means the agent was responsible for the activity which used the entity.

semanticText.definition: The entity is attributed to an agent to express the agent's responsibility for that entity, possibly along with other agents. This description can be understood as shorthand for saying that the agent was responsible for the activity which used the entity.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 wording points to responsibility for the use of an input entity in the Provenance activity.

impact.impactRationaleMd: No structure changed, but the directionality of the shorthand interpretation changed. Mapping logic, audit displays, and responsibility analytics that used the R4 wording can assign responsibility to the wrong activity relationship in R6.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Attribution of responsibility for a source entity versus a generated entity can matter in audit and accountability workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Align entity.agent with Provenance.entity as an entity used during the activity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Broaden the definition to explicitly cover both generated-entity attribution and responsibility for use, or add a separate element while keeping the old semantics.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Because `Provenance.entity` is an entity used in the activity, the R6 wording is a plausible correction or clarification. Existing systems that relied on the R4 generated-entity sentence can still experience semantic breakage, but preserving that wording unchanged would undermine the clearer R6 interpretation.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A partial base alternative would have described `entity.agent` as covering both responsibility for the entity's prior generation and responsibility for its use in the current activity, or introduced a distinct optional relationship while leaving the old interpretation intact. That would soften migration but at the cost of durable ambiguity and possible duplicate representations of attribution.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: A transitional semantic bridge would reduce surprise but leaves ambiguous or duplicate attribution relationships in a resource focused on entities used in the activity.

evidence.detail: R4 definition refers to the activity which generated the entity.
R6 definition refers to the activity which used the entity.

examples.examplesMd: The same JSON can validate in both versions while being interpreted differently, so no structural invalid example is shown.

findings.narrativeMd: The wording for `entity.agent` changes a key relationship direction: R4 describes responsibility for the activity that generated the entity, while R6 describes responsibility for the activity that used the entity. This is a semantic migration risk even though the element shape is unchanged.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Instances remain structurally valid, but behavior can differ in audit displays, responsibility calculations, and transformations that derive W3C PROV relationships. The risk is still-valid-but-behaviorally-different rather than old-valid/new-invalid.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review any mapping from `Provenance.entity.agent` to audit, PROV-O, or responsibility models. Confirm whether your R4 data used the field for source-entity custodianship, generation responsibility, or access mediation, and document the interpretation during migration.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: This appears to be a semantic clarification that could not be represented as a purely structural addition. A transition note would have helped identify affected mappings.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: R6 preserves the Provenance canonical URL, id/name/type, resource kind, non-abstract flag, derivation, and DomainResource base. Status/FMM metadata changed but is listed as non-breaking.
No local fixed[x], pattern[x], or defaultValue changes were found on Provenance elements.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraint changes were found.
No local Provenance element changed `isModifier`. The root/base `modifierExtension` metadata differences are inherited and excluded.
No local slicing discriminators, slice names, ordering, or slicing rules were introduced or removed.

`Provenance.occurred[x]` preserved its Period/dateTime choice types, and most local datatypes are unchanged. Material element replacement and reference-target changes are reported as findings rather than counted here as no-change.

No XML/JSON representation-format change was found for retained local elements. Serialization risks arise from removed/added element names and summary projection changes, which are reported separately.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Provenance maturity/status advanced in R6 ballot metadata
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The canonical URL, resource type, kind, baseDefinition, and derivation are unchanged. Status/FMM/standards-status metadata do not change instance wire validity by themselves.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Governance and conformance programs may treat the R6 resource as more stable/normative than the R4 draft/trial-use artifact.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Successor authorization field uses an example rather than extensible PurposeOfUse binding
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: A weaker example binding is not a base validation restriction. The breaking aspect is the removal of the R4 `reason` path, which is reported separately.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Systems that used R4 extensible-binding warnings for PurposeOfUse policy need to decide whether to preserve stricter local validation in R6 profiles.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Several comments normalize may/should to MAY/SHOULD wording
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Most observed capitalization changes do not alter computable cardinality, type, binding strength, or constraint severity.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Do not treat these editorial wording changes as local breaking changes unless a profile or business rule explicitly depends on the narrative sentence.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited DomainResource changes were visible in the snapshot, including contained-resource wording and dom-* constraint expression changes. They are intentionally excluded from this Provenance-local report.

Inherited ele-1/ext-1 constraint text and extension constraint differences appear on Provenance snapshots but are base datatype/extension concerns.

analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Consult the official FHIR change history, R6 ballot notes, and relevant HL7 Jira items for Provenance.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Local complete CodeSystems were compared for `provenance-entity-role`, but external terminology value sets such as PurposeOfUse, participation-role-type, and security-role-type were not expanded with a terminology server.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run terminology expansions for both versions with the appropriate THO/package dependencies and compare code membership and meanings.
